topics.name: The Ark of the Covenant
topics.intro: The ark was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the covenant, made at Sinai (Exodus 25) and carried before Israel until Solomon set it in the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 8). The Philistines took it and sent it back (1 Samuel 4-6), and David brought it up to Jerusalem. After that the Bible goes quiet. The last clear mention is Josiah telling the Levites to put it in the temple (2 Chronicles 35:3), Jeremiah says it won't be missed or made again (Jeremiah 3:16), and when Babylon strips the temple in 586 BC the list of what was taken doesn't name it (2 Kings 25:13-17). Every claim below starts in that silence.

claims.name: Kiriath-jearim (Deir el-Azar, Abu Ghosh)
claims.claim: The Bible says the ark rested here for twenty years before David moved it. Since 2017 a Tel Aviv University and Collège de France team has argued the hilltop held a monumental 8th century BC compound, possibly a temple for the ark built under Jeroboam II of Israel. Press headlines turned this into 'the ark may have been found', which the team never claimed.
claims.text: 1 Samuel 7:1-2: the men of Kirjath-jearim brought the ark 'into the house of Abinadab in the hill' and 'the ark abode in Kirjathjearim ... twenty years'. 2 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles 13 continue the story of David moving it (not quoted here).
claims.who: Shmunis Family Excavations, a joint Tel Aviv University and Collège de France project directed by Israel Finkelstein (Tel Aviv University), Thomas Römer and Christophe Nicolle (Collège de France), funded by Sana and Vlad Shmunis. The summit belongs to the Convent of the Ark of the Covenant (Sisters of St. Joseph of the Apparition).
claims.digging: Gabriel Barkay salvage excavation 1995-1996. Shmunis excavations: two four-week seasons, August 2017 and August 2019, on the slopes (not the convent summit, which could not be dug), plus a seismic-geodetic study (2017) and ground penetrating radar. Final report published 2025 (TAU Monograph 45; Penn State UP open access, on MUSE February 2026). I found no announcement of any field season after 2019. None now, as checked 2026-10-20. A lecture on 17 August 2026 by Anselm Hagedorn argues for a different identification (Tel Moza), but that is a lecture, not a dig.

claims.for: The identification of Deir el-Azar with biblical Kiriath-jearim is treated as secure by the excavators on the basis of the tribal border lists (Joshua 15:8-10; 18:14-16) among other arguments. The hill has an artificial-looking flat platform about 150 by 110 m, and seismic work found fills up to six metres deep, which the team reads as a monumental podium. They date its walls by OSL and pottery to the early Iron IIB (first half of the 8th century BC) and argue, in Biblica 2020, that the older ark narrative (1 Samuel 4:1-7:1) reflects the ideology of Jeroboam II, whose kingdom dominated Judah after Joash defeated Amaziah (2 Kings 14:11-13). On that reading the site really did house an ark shrine, and the biblical tradition that the ark rested here preserves a real cult place.
claims.against: No ark, no ark furniture and no temple building were found; the summit itself, where any shrine stood, lies under the convent and was not excavated, and the excavators say even a summit dig might not give significant results because of erosion and fill. The Jeroboam II temple is an interpretation of retaining walls, not a found sanctuary. Yigal Levin challenges the excavators' reading of the site's character and purpose in Iron II and re-examines its tribal setting. Anselm Hagedorn (Osnabrück, Protestant theology) argues the biblical town was not Deir el-Azar at all but Tel Moza. From the other side, readers who take 1 Samuel at face value object that the team's own dating puts the platform about two centuries after David, so it cannot be the place 1 Samuel 7 describes; the TAU Institute for Advanced Studies summary of the team's view says the site was built about two centuries after David's reign, against 1 Samuel 7, and Finkelstein and Römer read the ark story as 8th to 7th century political literature. Danny Herman, a guide who accepts the biblical account, calls conclusions drawn from a small section of retaining wall too speculative, and suggests the 8th century platform could commemorate an earlier ark site rather than disprove it.

claims.name: Under the Temple Mount, Jerusalem (Chamber of the Wood)
claims.claim: The ark never left the Temple Mount: King Josiah (or Solomon) hid it in an underground chamber, and it is still there under the Haram al-Sharif. This is the main rabbinic tradition and is held today by some Temple movement rabbis.
claims.text: Mishnah Shekalim 6:1-2: the households of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Hananya bowed at a fourteenth place, 'facing the wood depository', because of a tradition 'that the Ark was sequestered there'; a priest who noticed an odd flagstone died before he could finish telling of it. Yoma 52b: Josiah buried the ark, with the jar of manna, the anointing oil, Aaron's staff and the Philistines' chest, citing 2 Chronicles 35:3. Yoma 53b-54a: Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish says 'the Ark was buried in its place' (from 1 Kings 8:8, 'they are there unto this day'), and 'the Rabbis say' it was buried in the Chamber of the Woodshed; this is set against Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, who say it went to Babylon. Mishnah Yoma 5:2: in the Second Temple there was only a stone, the even shetiyah, where the ark had been. Note: the pin placed here is the Pleiades point for the Second Temple, a general marker; the Mishnah's chamber has no known location.
claims.who: Rabbinic tradition (Mishnah, Tosefta as cited in Yoma 54a, Babylonian Talmud). In modern times Rabbi Yehuda Meir Getz, rabbi of the Western Wall (died 1995), and Rabbi Chaim Richman (Temple Institute), who told The Jewish Press in 2020 'We basically know where the ark is located'.
claims.digging: No excavation of the platform interior is known; the Islamic Waqf administers the compound and limits access (Temple Mount Sifting Project), and a BAR editorial sidebar (undated) said not even a non-invasive archaeological survey had been done since 1967. The 1981 Getz tunnel (separate entry) is the only known attempt aimed at the ark, and it was sealed. In October 1999 Waqf earthworks removed about 10,000 tons of fill, now sifted off-site by the Temple Mount Sifting Project; that is salvage of dumped soil, not a search for the ark. None now, as checked 2026-10-20; I found no 2025-2026 report of any excavation on the platform.
published_press: The Jewish Press, Tzvi Fishman, 13 March 2020 (Richman, Adiel Getz).
Aish.com, Avi Abrams (undated).
Temple Mount Sifting Project website (background on the 1999 earthworks).
claims.for: This is the oldest documented Jewish tradition on the question, recorded in the Mishnah and attributed to the households of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Hananya the deputy High Priest, and it names a specific spot (the wood chamber) and a specific family custom of bowing there. 2 Chronicles 35:3 shows Josiah giving orders about the ark late in the monarchy, which the Talmud reads as a hiding order, and 2 Kings 25:13-17 lists the temple items carried to Babylon without the ark. 1 Kings 8:8 says the poles are 'there unto this day'. Because the platform has never been excavated, the claim has never been tested and cannot be ruled out.
claims.against: The same Talmud passage records the opposite view held by Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai (exile to Babylon), and the Talmud itself refutes the 'to this day means forever' argument from 1 Kings 8:8 with counter-examples (Judges 1:21; 1 Chronicles 4:42-43). The Mishnah stories are pious legend with no physical evidence. Jeremiah 3:16 speaks of a time when the ark will not 'come to mind', which many read as the ark already being gone. Within the believing Jewish world, the Lubavitcher Rebbe answered Rabbi Getz in 1976 that excavation was not permitted because it was 'a matter of Kodeshim', and Getz's own family says he kept the dig from the prime minister. Practically, no excavation is possible under the status quo, so the claim is untestable.

claims.name: Warren's Gate tunnel, Western Wall Tunnels, Jerusalem
claims.claim: In July 1981 the rabbi of the Western Wall, Yehuda Getz, broke into a sealed gate under the Temple Mount and dug eastward toward the Holy of Holies hoping to reach the ark, until the government sealed it.
claims.text: No ancient text names this gate as the ark's location; the motive came from the rabbinic tradition that the ark is hidden under the Mount (Mishnah Shekalim 6:1-2; Yoma 53b-54a).
claims.who: Rabbi Yehuda Meir Getz (rabbi of the Western Wall, died 1995), with workers from the Western Wall tunnel project. His grandson Rabbi Adiel Getz is the main source for the inside account (Jewish Press, 2020).
claims.digging: July 1981: workers broke through the gate, drained a water-filled cistern and cleared a passage; clashes followed underground, and Prime Minister Menachem Begin ordered it sealed; it was closed with concrete. The Jewish Press article calls the gate 'Wilson's Gate', which appears to be an error for Warren's Gate (Wilson's Arch is a different feature); Aish.com and other accounts say Warren's Gate. A claim that in 1983 Getz and Rabbi Shlomo Goren said they saw the ark appears only in Wikipedia-derived text I could not trace to a primary source, so it is not included as fact. None now, as checked 2026-10-20: the passage remains sealed and unexplored.
published_press: The Jewish Press, 13 March 2020.
Aish.com (undated).
Emek Shaveh / Jerusalem Map, 'The Western Wall Tunnels' (states Begin ordered the tunnel sealed).
claims.for: The gate is a real Second Temple period entrance that led into the Mount close to the area of the Holy of Holies, so a tunnel behind it is the most direct route anyone has had toward the place the rabbinic tradition points to. Getz's workers reported hollow sounds beyond a wall before work stopped. It was stopped for political reasons, not because anything was disproved.
claims.against: Nothing was found, and no archaeologist published any data. The Aish author concedes 'we don't know whether or not the Ark ... was in that particular shaft'. The Lubavitcher Rebbe had refused Getz permission in 1976, and the dig was unlicensed and secret even from the prime minister by Getz's family's own account. The tunnel's direction and the theory behind it rest on a tradition that the Talmud itself disputes.

claims.name: Mount Nebo, Jordan (Jeremiah's cave)
claims.claim: Before the Babylonian destruction, the prophet Jeremiah carried the tabernacle, the ark and the incense altar to the mountain Moses climbed (Nebo) and sealed them in a cave, to stay hidden until God gathers his people again.
claims.text: 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 (KJV Apocrypha): Jeremiah, 'being warned of God, commanded the tabernacle and the ark to go with him, as he went forth into the mountain, where Moses climbed up', found 'an hollow cave' and put in 'the tabernacle, and the ark, and the altar of incense, and so stopped the door'; followers could not find it again, and Jeremiah said 'that place ... shall be unknown until the time that God gather his people again together'. The mountain is identified by Deuteronomy 34:1: 'the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah'. 2 Maccabees cites this as 'found in the records' (2:1, 4), i.e. an earlier written source it does not name. The pin is the Pleiades point for Mount Nebo; the text gives no cave location.
claims.who: The author of 2 Maccabees (Hellenistic Jewish work; the letter in chapters 1-2 is addressed to Jews in Egypt). 2 Maccabees is canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and apocryphal for Jews and Protestants. Later searchers include Antonia Futterer (1920s) and Tom Crotser (1981, separate entry), and an Adventist lay group (Ron Spear and others) that entered a cave near the Franciscan monastery in June 1982.
claims.digging: No licensed excavation has ever targeted the ark here. Futterer explored a cave in the 1920s. Crotser broke into a chamber in 1981 without a permit. In June 1982 an Adventist lay group (Spear, Newhart and others) distracted a guard and was lowered into a chamber about 300 feet from the Franciscan monastery; they found no tunnel. Jordanian authorities cancelled Andrews University's licensed Madaba Plains Project in 1982 and 1983, partly because of unauthorized ark-hunting near Nebo (Spectrum). None now, as checked 2026-10-20 (I found no current ark-related dig).
published_press: Spectrum 13 (1982-1983), Patti Hansen Tompkins, 'Adventist Raiders of the Lost Ark'.
Biblical Archaeology Review, May/June 1983, on Crotser and Futterer.
claims.for: This is the only ancient text that actually narrates where the ark went, and it says it draws on earlier written records (2:1, 4). Jeremiah was in Jerusalem at the fall of the city, and Nebo is within reach east of the Jordan. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians it is Scripture. The text also explains why no one has found it: the place was meant to stay unknown until God reveals it (2:7-8).
claims.against: 2 Maccabees presents this as a quoted tradition inside a festal letter, mixed with the legend of the hidden fire (2:1, 10), and the Jewish and Protestant traditions do not treat the book as Scripture. Jeremiah 3:16 has Jeremiah himself saying the ark will no longer be remembered. The Talmud, which knew other traditions, does not mention Nebo and puts the ark under the Temple or in Babylon. No licensed archaeologist has found any trace, and the text itself says the site cannot be found by searching. David McCreery, director of ACOR in Amman, noted in 1982 that ark-hunters 'arrive and depart on a fairly regular basis'.

claims.name: Mount Pisgah cave, Nebo ridge, Jordan (Tom Crotser)
claims.claim: In 1981 Tom Crotser of Winfield, Kansas said he broke through a wall inside a cave on Mount Pisgah and saw the gold-covered ark, and took colour photographs of it.
claims.text: Based on 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 and Deuteronomy 34:1 (Nebo / Pisgah). Earlier, Antonia Frederick Futterer, an American explorer, searched Nebo for the ark in the 1920s; his 1927 pamphlet described a cave corridor with 'hieroglyphics' ending at two doors, and his sketches guided Crotser (BAR 1983).
claims.who: Tom Crotser, Institute for Restoring Ancient History International (Winfield, Kansas), November 1981 (BAR gives the date of the cave entry as Halloween, 31 October 1981). Crotser also claimed to have found the Tower of Babel and Noah's Ark. Newspaper accounts said he wanted the ark to help restore the Temple before a Second Coming he predicted for September or October 1988.
claims.digging: 1981: Crotser entered the cave without a permit and broke through a wall into a chamber. David McCreery (director, American Center of Oriental Research, Amman) said neither he nor the director-general of the Jordanian Department of Antiquities (Dr. Hadidi) had heard of the group and that it was 'illegal to excavate without a permit'. April 11, 1982: Adventist archaeologist Siegfried Horn spent an hour and a half with Crotser examining the evidence. None now, as checked 2026-10-20. Exact cave location was never published, so no coordinates are given.
published_press: Biblical Archaeology Review, May/June 1983, 'Tom Crotser Has Found the Ark of the Covenant, Or Has He?' (subtitle: a false report of an ark sighting led to the cancellation of an American excavation).
Spectrum 13 (1982-1983), 'Adventist Raiders of the Lost Ark'.
claims.for: Crotser said he had eyewitnesses and colour photographs, and the location fits 2 Maccabees and Deuteronomy 34:1. Some sympathetic Adventists who interviewed his team in 1981 concluded it did not appear to be a hoax.
claims.against: Siegfried Horn, a respected Adventist archaeologist who shared the group's belief in the Bible and was paid by fellow Adventists to check the claim, concluded that what the Kansas group had found 'was not an ancient artifact and therefore could not be the Ark of the Covenant'. The work was illegal under Jordanian law. Crotser's record of other claimed finds undercut his credibility, and BAR reported that the affair contributed to the cancellation of a legitimate American excavation (Andrews University's project, per Spectrum). No object was ever produced.

claims.name: Axum (Aksum), Ethiopia: Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion / Chapel of the Tablet
claims.claim: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that the original ark (or the tablets of the law) was brought from Jerusalem by Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and is kept today in the Chapel of the Tablet beside the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, guarded by a single monk.
claims.text: Kebra Nagast (tr. Budge 1922), chapter 48 and the chapters around it: Azaryas, son of the high priest Zadok, has a carpenter make wooden boards of the ark's size; an angel opens the sanctuary doors; Azaryas and his companions take 'Zion, the Tabernacle of the Law of God' and leave the boards covered with its covering in its place; later Zadok finds 'nothing except the wooden boards'. In the Kebra Nagast the ark goes with Menelik to Ethiopia. The Bible does not say this; 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9 tell of the Queen of Sheba's visit without any son or ark (not quoted here).
claims.who: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church; the guardian monk (appointed for life by his predecessor) is the only person allowed to see the object. Patriarch Abune Paulos said in Rome in June 2009 that he had seen it and that the world would soon see it; the promised announcement did not happen.
claims.digging: No excavation of the church or chapel is allowed and no scholar has examined the object. Separately, in spring 2008 a University of Hamburg team under Helmut Ziegert dug at Axum-Dungur and announced (press release, 7 May 2008) a 10th century BC 'palace of the Queen of Sheba' with an altar where the ark 'could have been kept for a time'; I found no peer-reviewed publication of this, and the claim was not about finding the ark. Axum suffered a massacre of hundreds of civilians on 28-29 November 2020 during the Tigray war (Amnesty International; AP), including at the church compound. None now, as checked 2026-10-20.
published_peer: Pierluigi Piovanelli, 'The Apocryphal Legitimation of a Solomonic Dynasty in the Kebra Nagast: A Reappraisal', Aethiopica 16 (2013) 7-44 (reads the Kebra Nagast as an early 14th century work for the Solomonic elite).
published_press: Stuart Munro-Hay, The Quest for the Ark of the Covenant (I.B. Tauris, 2005), book (via Publishers Weekly review).
Graham Hancock, The Sign and the Seal (Crown, 1992), book.

claims.for: Ethiopia has a continuous, nationally central tradition: every Ethiopian Orthodox church has a tabot (altar tablet) understood as a replica of the ark, and the Axum church has claimed the ark itself since at least the 16th century (Munro-Hay, per PW). The Hebrew Bible never records the ark's fate, so a removal before 586 BC cannot be ruled out from Scripture. The custodians say the object exists and the patriarch said he saw it. Milton Fisher, an OT professor who lived in Ethiopia twelve years, wrote that he could not easily dismiss the Ethiopian traditions and testimony.
claims.against: No outsider has been allowed to examine it, so the claim cannot be tested. The only scholar known to have seen the object, Edward Ullendorff (SOAS), who saw it as a British officer in 1941, told the Los Angeles Times in 1992 it was of 'middle-to late-medieval construction', and told Tudor Parfitt it was like the model arks in other Ethiopian churches. The Kebra Nagast is late: Budge's preface notes the colophons place the Arabic translation between AD 1314 and 1344 and the Ethiopic one after that, and Piovanelli reads it as early 14th century dynastic propaganda. Grierson notes the earliest report of the ark in Ethiopia dates to the late 12th century, and that the clergy speak of a tablet, not a box. Munro-Hay concluded the church never held the ark but an altar stone. Bible-believing critics also reject it: Milton Fisher (Philadelphia Theological Seminary) criticised Hancock's 'imaginative stringing of the beads'; Ephraim Isaac (as quoted by Brian King, 1999) asked for the tradition to be respected but warned against 'wild guesses' about the object. The 2009 promise to show it was withdrawn.

claims.name: Tana Qirqos island, Lake Tana, Ethiopia
claims.claim: The ark rested on the island monastery of Tana Qirqos for centuries before it was taken to Axum. Graham Hancock's The Sign and the Seal (1992) made this a waystation on his proposed route Jerusalem, Elephantine, Tana Qirqos, Axum.
claims.text: No biblical or ancient text. The source is the oral tradition of the island's monks.
claims.who: Monks of Tana Qirqos (Ethiopian Orthodox; the island is closed to women per the Comboni report). Graham Hancock, The Sign and the Seal: The Quest for the Lost Ark of the Covenant (1992; Crown in the US per library catalogue entries seen in search results, not opened). The BASE Institute (Fox News / The Sun, 2018) repeated the Nile-to-Lake-Tana route.
claims.digging: No excavation for the ark known. Hancock visited and reported sacrificial stones with blood-collecting holes (as summarised by Manera on grahamhancock.com, 2021). None now, as checked 2026-10-20. Coordinates left null: two OpenStreetMap records for Tana Qirqos (an islet and a place of worship) are about 8 km apart, so I could not fix the site reliably.

claims.for: The monks have a long-held local tradition that the ark was kept there (the Comboni writers report it as the place where 'the Arc of the Covenant was preserved'), and visitors report old sacrificial installations of a Judaic type. claims.text: No ancient text says the ark was at Elephantine. The Elephantine papyri (5th century BC Aramaic documents) show a Jewish temple there where sacrifices were offered (per Porten). The Bible records no removal under Manasseh.
claims.who: Graham Hancock, The Sign and the Seal (1992). Assessed by Bezalel Porten (Hebrew University), 'Did the Ark Stop at Elephantine?', BAR 21.3 (1995).
claims.digging: The island has long been excavated for its own sake (temple remains and papyri), but no excavation has looked for or found any trace of the ark. None now for the ark, as checked 2026-10-20.

claims.for: A real Jewish temple with animal sacrifice stood at Elephantine in the 6th and 5th centuries BC, outside Jerusalem, which is unusual and needs explaining. claims.name: Babylon (taken in the conquest of 597/586 BC)
claims.claim: Nebuchadnezzar's army took or destroyed the ark with the other temple treasures when Jerusalem fell (597 and 586 BC), so it went to Babylon or was broken up for its gold.
claims.text: 2 Kings 24:13 (597 BC): Nebuchadnezzar 'carried out thence all the treasures of the house of the Lord ... and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold which Solomon king of Israel had made'. 2 Kings 25:13-17 (586 BC) lists the bronze pillars, bases, sea, pots, shovels, firepans and bowls, with no ark. 2 Chronicles 36:10, 18: 'the goodly vessels' and 'all the vessels of the house of God, great and small ... he brought to Babylon'. Ezra 1:7-11 lists 5,400 returned vessels, with no ark. 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 10:22: 'the ark of our covenant is spoiled'. Babylonian Talmud Yoma 53b: Rabbi Eliezer says 'The Ark was exiled to Babylonia' (2 Chronicles 36:10) and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai agrees (Isaiah 39:6), against Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish (hidden in its place). Mishnah Yoma 5:2 begins 'After the Ark was taken'. Revelation 11:19 places 'the ark of his testament' in the heavenly temple.
claims.who: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai (Talmud, Yoma 53b); the author of 4 Ezra (2 Esdras 3-14). The pin is the Pleiades point for the city of Babylon.
claims.digging: I found no dig at Babylon aimed at the ark. None now for the ark, as checked 2026-10-20.
published_press: Gary Byers, Associates for Biblical Research, 2008 (lists Babylon among proposed fates and concludes no one knows).
claims.for: This is the simplest reading of the biblical evidence: the Babylonians looted and cut up the temple's gold (2 Kings 24:13), 2 Chronicles says 'all the vessels ... great and small' went to Babylon, and the ark is never heard of again in the narrative. Jeremiah 3:16 expects a future without the ark. The Second Temple had no ark (Mishnah Yoma 5:2). A first-century Jewish apocalypse (4 Ezra 10:22) says the ark was 'spoiled'. Respected Talmudic sages held it went to Babylon.
claims.against: None of the detailed inventories (2 Kings 25:13-17; Ezra 1:9-11) names the ark, which is strange for the most important object in the temple if it was carried off; that silence is what the hiding traditions (Talmud, 2 Maccabees) build on. The Talmud records Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish and 'the Rabbis' saying it was hidden instead. 4 Ezra is a visionary lament, not a report. So the Babylon view is a reasonable inference, not a documented event.

topics.name: Noah's Ark
topics.intro: Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, plural. Ararat is the Hebrew name for Urartu, the kingdom around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey, Armenia and north-west Iran, so the text names a region, not a peak; the single mountain called Ararat today got that name much later. Older Jewish and Syriac tradition put the landing further south (the Targums say the mountains of Qardu), at the mountain now called Cudi Dag, which is also where the Quran puts it (11:44). The claims below are the places people have searched.

claims.name: Durupınar formation (Doğubayazıt, Türkiye)
claims.coord_source: OpenStreetMap way 144047151, tagged 'Durupınar sitesi', Üzengili, Doğubayazıt, Ağrı (centroid from Nominatim, checked 2026-10-20). Not from an excavation report.
claims.claim: A boat-shaped mound about 157 m long, about 29 to 30 km south of the Ararat summit, is the buried remains of Noah's ark. Its backers say 2026 radar and core drilling found no bedrock inside, a hard layer that broke a drill bit, and organic-rich layers.
claims.text: Genesis 8:4 says the ark rested 'upon the mountains of Ararat' (plural): a region, not one named peak. Encyclopaedia Judaica identifies biblical Ararat with Urartu, the kingdom centred on Lake Van, and notes the Bible names no specific mountain. 2 Kings 19:37 and Jeremiah 51:27 use Ararat for a land and a kingdom.
claims.who: Spotted on aerial photos in 1959 by Turkish Army Captain İlhan Durupınar. Promoted from 1977 by Ron Wyatt; studied by David Fasold from 1985 (nine trips; book 'The Ark of Noah', 1988). Since about 2021 promoted by Noah's Ark Scans (founder Andrew Jones, a software developer and not an archaeologist). 2022 to 2023: Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University and Istanbul Technical University sampling team (Vice Rector Prof. Faruk Kaya). 2026: field program led by Prof. Dr. Cenker Atila (Archaeology, Sivas Cumhuriyet University) with about 20 scientists and students from five countries, supported by Noah's Ark Scans; radar by Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar (Bakhtar Research and Engineering).
claims.digging: 1960: US-sponsored survey (Vandeman, Brandenberger) found no sign of human work. 1985 to 1988: Wyatt and Fasold radar; 1987 radar by Tom Fenner could not reproduce earlier records; 1987 to 1988 magnetometer, radar, seismic and core drilling (Baumgardner), four holes to about 10 m, mudflow clay over basalt or bedrock, no wood. 2022 to 2023: about 30 soil and rock samples tested at ITU, dated 3,500 to 5,000 years, with Kaya saying the dating cannot show a ship is there. 2024: Noah's Ark Scans soil survey (88 samples, 22 sites) claimed about three times more organic matter inside. 2026: fieldwork 29 June to 11 September under Turkish permits (Atila says from two ministries; ministries not named); GPS, 2D/3D modelling, GPR, resistivity, dry percussion core drilling to up to 18 m inside and outside the outline (Fox News reports about 20 m in places); a bit broke at about 4 to 5 m in one hole inside the formation. Lab work through winter 2026 to 2027; full data targeted for May 2027; a book 'Durupınar Formasyonu 2026 Yılı Araştırmaları' and three papers promised. ACTIVE NOW.
published_peer: Collins, L. G. and Fasold, D. F. (1996), 'Bogus Noah's Ark from Turkey exposed as a common geologic structure', Journal of Geoscience Education 44: 439-444. Concludes the formation is a natural doubly plunging syncline; 'iron brackets' are goethite and limonite; 'anchor stones' are local andesite; no fossil wood or elemental carbon found.
No peer-reviewed paper from the 2022 to 2026 work had been published as of 2026-10-20.

claims.for: The length (about 157 to 164 m) matches 300 cubits if a long (Egyptian) cubit of about 52 cm is used. The project says 2026 holes inside the outline hit soil, sediment, organic-rich layers and cavities, not bedrock or a solid limestone block, and that a layer 'harder than limestone' broke a percussion bit; it proposes petrified or mineralised wood, to be tested by a third-party lab. Its radar (BakhtarRadar, GPR, ERT) shows linear features, right angles, layering and possible voids that it reads as corridors, compartments and decks. 2024 soil sampling claimed about three times more organic matter inside than outside. The 2026 work is a permitted program under a Turkish state university archaeologist, not an amateur dig, and the team says it has not claimed an intact wooden ship and will issue a statement only after lab work.
claims.against: The only peer-reviewed study (Collins and Fasold 1996) calls it a natural syncline, and Fasold, its main early champion, co-wrote that paper and repudiated the site in sworn testimony in 1997. Earlier 'petrified wood', 'iron brackets' and 'anchor stones' were identified as basalt, goethite or limonite, and local andesite; Wyatt's prize wood sample was never sectioned. A fossiliferous limestone bed crosses the site. Critics who believe in Noah and the ark reject it: Andrew Snelling (Answers in Genesis, young-earth geologist) argues the radar 'tunnels' and 'cabins' may reflect jointing, layering and dissolution channels in limestone, and that a site in a deep valley on Ararat's southern slopes conflicts with Genesis 8:4; Ken Ham concludes 'both the location and the geology discount' it; Wesley Huff calls the claims 'not legit', notes the team has no trained archaeologists and that 'it looks like a boat' is not evidence; Jeremiah Johnston says it is 'not the spot of Noah's ark'. Turkish geologist Murat Avcı reads it as a landslide block shaped by natural processes. A broken drill bit shows hardness, not wood; proof needs recovered wood cell structure. The 2023 ITU dating showed human activity in the area, not a ship. All 2026 claims are from the project and its press, with lab results pending.

topics.name: Mount Sinai
topics.intro: The mountain where God gave the law is called both Sinai and Horeb (Exodus 19; Deuteronomy 5:2), the mountain of God (Exodus 3:1). The text gives the stages of the journey from Egypt (Numbers 33) but nothing a surveyor could use, and Paul's Mount Sinai in Arabia (Galatians 4:25) has been read both ways, since Arabia in his day took in the Sinai peninsula. The traditional peak, Jebel Musa, goes back to fourth-century monks; the main alternatives are in Saudi Arabia and the Negev. OpenBible's data scores Jebel Musa highest, but short of the line it uses for a secure identification.

claims.claim: The traditional Mount Sinai, where Moses received the law, is Jebel Musa in the granite massif of southern Sinai, with St Catherine's Monastery at the site of the burning bush.
claims.text: Scripture calls it both Sinai and Horeb, 'the mountain of God' (Exodus 3:1; 1 Kings 19:8). Moses first reaches it while pasturing Jethro's flock, Jethro being 'the priest of Midian' (Exodus 3:1). Deuteronomy 1:2: 'eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea'. Exodus 19:18: the mountain 'all in smoke' because Yahweh 'descended upon it in fire'. Galatians 4:25: 'Mount Sinai in Arabia'. Exodus 18:27: Jethro leaves Moses and goes 'into his own land'. Egeria (late 4th century; the monastery dates her visit to about 380) climbed the mountain with resident monks, saw a small church on the summit and 'the cave where holy Moses was', a church at the Bush, and was shown Horeb and Elijah's cave and the place 'where the calf was made'.
claims.who: Monastic tradition from the 3rd to 4th centuries (the monastery dates Sinai monasticism to the 3rd century; Empress Helen is said to have supported it in the 4th); Justinian built the basilica and fortress walls in the 6th century. Modern proponents listed by BAS include Edward Robinson (1838), Samuel Bartlett (1879), J. Simons (1959); Ras Safsafa (part of the massif) by E. H. Palmer. James Hoffmeier supports the southern Sinai location (per Answers in Genesis).
claims.digging: No archaeological excavation aimed at the Exodus was found for 2025 to 2026. Egypt's 'Great Transfiguration' tourism project (launched 2021) is building around St Catherine; on 28 May 2025 the Ismailia Court of Appeal ruled the monastery's surrounding lands are state property under oversight of the antiquities and environment ministries, leaving the monks religious use of the churches. None now (construction and legal dispute only).
published_peer: No peer-reviewed find links Jebel Musa to the Exodus. BAS: no Exodus-related remains from the traditional date (about 1200 BCE) have been found in the Sinai Peninsula.
published_press: Egeria, travel account (4th century), McClure and Feltoe translation (1919).

claims.for: It has the oldest continuous site tradition of any candidate (4th century, attested by an eyewitness pilgrim), a great plain below the massif where a large group could camp, and it lies in the peninsula the Israelites crossed after leaving Egypt. Hoffmeier and many 19th and 20th century geographers accepted it.
claims.against: The tradition is at least 1,500 years after the events and arose with Byzantine monasticism; Anati says it 'is not corroborated by biblical accounts'. Turpin (Answers in Genesis, a fellow believer) notes it is about 225 miles from Midian and about 160 miles from Kadesh-barnea, which strains the 11-day journey of Deuteronomy 1:2, and its main support is 'Christian tradition from the fourth century AD'. No Late Bronze Age Israelite remains have been found there.

topics.name: Sodom and the cities of the plain
topics.intro: Genesis puts Sodom and the other cities of the plain in the well-watered circle of the Jordan that Lot could see from near Bethel (Genesis 13:10-12), and places the battle of the kings in the valley of Siddim, "that is, the Salt Sea" (Genesis 14:3). That leaves two broad candidates: the plain north of the Dead Sea, where the view from Bethel points, and the south end, where Early Bronze Age towns were destroyed and burned. Both have serious defenders, and both have a dating problem.

claims.name: Tall el-Hammam
claims.coord_source: OpenStreetMap way 656094631, tagged historic=archaeological_site, name 'Tall el Hammam' (centroid as returned by Nominatim). The 2021 Scientific Reports paper (Fig. 4 caption) gives 31 deg 50.483 N, 35 deg 40.029 E (31.8414, 35.6672) as the centre of its Google Earth base image; the two points are about 650 m apart.
claims.claim: The large Middle Bronze Age city at Tall el-Hammam, in the Jordan Valley northeast of the Dead Sea, is biblical Sodom, and its fiery destruction layer is the destruction of Genesis 19.
claims.text: Lot 'saw all the valley of the Jordan, that it was well watered everywhere' and 'lived in the cities of the valley and moved his tents as far as Sodom' (Genesis 13:10-12). The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar) gathered 'to the valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea)' (Genesis 14:2-3). 'Yahweh rained on Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire ... and He overthrew those cities, and all the valley' (Genesis 19:24-25); Abraham saw 'the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace' (Genesis 19:28). Scripture names no site and gives no absolute date.
claims.who: Steven Collins, director and chief archaeologist of the Tall el-Hammam Excavation Project (TeHEP), a joint project of Trinity Southwest University (Albuquerque) and Veritas International University under the Department of Antiquities of Jordan. Collins has argued the identification since the 2000s, including Biblical Archaeology Review (March/April 2013, 'Where Is Sodom?' with the sidebar 'North vs. South') and the book Discovering the City of Sodom (Howard Books, 2013, with Latayne C. Scott). Phillip J. Silvia (TeHEP Director of Scientific Analysis) is a co-author of the airburst papers.
claims.digging: Season 1 ran 9 Dec 2005 to 10 Jan 2006 (project site); annual seasons followed (Eisenbrauns says excavation began 2005-2006 and continued annually; Sci.News in 2021 said fifteen consecutive seasons since 2006). The project's own site advertises a field school for 29 January to 9 February 2023 and a 2023 dig schedule; it lists nothing later. No 2024, 2025 or 2026 season could be verified. Status now: not verified.
published_peer: Collins, Kobs and Luddeni, The Tall al-Hammam Excavations, Volume 1 (Eisenbrauns, 2015): ceramics of seven seasons (2005-2011) and artifacts of eight seasons (2005-2012). An excavation report; the publisher's page does not mention Sodom.
The airburst paper and its retraction are listed under the separate 'tall-el-hammam-airburst' entry.
published_press: Biblical Archaeology Review 39:2 (2013), 'Where Is Sodom?' with sidebar 'North vs. South: Why the Southern Location Doesn't Work' (popular magazine, not peer reviewed).
Collins and Scott, Discovering the City of Sodom (Howard Books, 2013), a trade book.

Collins's replies to critics in TSU's in-house Biblical Research Bulletin, e.g. 'A Response to Bryant G. Wood's Critique of Collins' Northern Sodom Theory' (BRB VII.7, 2007) and 'Tall el-Hammam Is Sodom: Billington's Heshbon Identification Suffers from Numerous Fatal Flaws' (BRB XII.1, 2012), as listed on the TeHEP site.
claims.for: Collins argues that nothing in the Bible points south and everything points to the area north of the Dead Sea: Genesis 13 has Lot look from the Bethel and Ai area over the 'valley of the Jordan' (the kikkar), which he takes as the circular plain north of the Dead Sea; most nineteenth century explorer-scholars (Conder, Tristram, Grove) put the cities there; Genesis 19:1 places the angels in the 'gate of Sodom' and TeHEP has excavated a major gate complex, with nothing similar in the south; Tall el-Hammam is about 100 acres, the largest Bronze Age site in the Jordan rift, against about 12 acres at Bab edh-Dhra, and is surrounded by satellite towns; Lot would have had no reason to pass the well-watered northern plain for the Lisan area. The final Middle Bronze Age stratum is a heavy ash and destruction layer, followed by centuries of regional abandonment. On chronology Collins replies that 'the Bronze Age patriarchal numbers cannot be equated in any way with our modern concept of absolute dating.'
claims.against: Chronology: the destruction-layer pottery dates to about 1650-1600 BC, which conventional biblical chronology puts only about two centuries before the Exodus (Christianity Today, 2014). Eugene Merrill (Dallas Theological Seminary, Artifax, Autumn 2012) argues the best manuscripts and sound hermeneutics demand an overthrow of Sodom at 2081 BC, which removes Tall el-Hammam from consideration; Todd Bolen summarises Merrill as saying the identification requires one to deny all biblical dates before the judges. Bryant Wood (Associates for Biblical Research, Bible and Spade 20:3, 2007) puts the biblical date at 2067 BC on a 430-year sojourn (Exodus 12:40), against 1852 BC on Collins's shortened 215-year sojourn. Simon Turpin (Answers in Genesis UK) says the identification would require revising the Exodus date. Geography: Wood argues Genesis 10:19 runs the border of Canaan south toward the cities, the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:3) is the southern basin, Ezekiel 16:46 places Sodom south of Jerusalem, Josephus, Eusebius and the Madaba Map put Zoar south of the Dead Sea, and the bitumen and sulphur fit the south; Bill Schlegel (Satellite Bible Atlas) argues the Genesis wording does not fit Tall el-Hammam. Stratigraphy: Wood said in 2007 that a site-wide destruction at the right date had not been demonstrated. Bolen adds that if the theory is right the Bible would be unreliable on times and places, the reverse of Collins's apologetic claim. James Hoffmeier (Trinity Evangelical Divinity School, emeritus) said dramatic claims by an archaeologist without credentials raise suspicions. Clyde Billington (Artifax) argued Tall el-Hammam is another site (Collins's reply title names Heshbon). These critics largely share Collins's belief in a historical Sodom; their objection is that his site breaks the biblical numbers.

claims.name: Tall el-Hammam (airburst)
claims.coord_source: Same site as tall-el-hammam-sodom: OpenStreetMap way 656094631.
claims.claim: A Tunguska-class cosmic airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam about 1650 BC, and this event may lie behind the Sodom account in Genesis.
claims.text: 'Yahweh rained on Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from Yahweh out of heaven' (Genesis 19:24); 'the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace' (Genesis 19:28). The text describes fire from heaven; it does not describe an airburst, and it names no site.
claims.who: Ted E. Bunch, Malcolm A. LeCompte, James P. Kennett, Allen West (Comet Research Group) and others, with Phillip J. Silvia (Trinity Southwest University), 21 authors. Published Scientific Reports, 20 September 2021. An expanded version (LeCompte, Collins, Silvia, Kletetschka, Witwer, Hermes, Moore, Wolbach and others) appeared in 2025 in Airbursts and Cratering Impacts (ScienceOpen).
claims.digging: No separate dig; samples come from TeHEP excavations at Tall el-Hammam (see tall-el-hammam-sodom). No current fieldwork verified.
published_peer: Bunch et al., 'A Tunguska sized airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam a Middle Bronze Age city in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea', Scientific Reports 11:18632 (20 Sep 2021), doi 10.1038/s41598-021-97778-3. RETRACTED 24 April 2025.

Author Correction, Scientific Reports 12:3265 (22 Feb 2022): figure panels across dozens of figures had been 'manipulated to remove the features irrelevant to the scientific content' (tape measures, labels, fingers); the authors called this 'inappropriate' and supplied originals.

Author Correction, Scientific Reports 13:8280 (22 May 2023): the paper had wrongly presented Mark Boslough's Sandia simulation (Fig. 53) as a model of Tunguska; it was a much larger hypothetical 15-megaton event. The subsection 'Comparison of TeH to the Tunguska airburst' was removed.
Jaret and Harris, 'No mineralogic or geochemical evidence of impact at Tall el-Hammam', Scientific Reports 12:5189 (25 Mar 2022), Matters Arising.

Boslough and Bruno, 'Misunderstandings about the Tunguska event, shock wave physics, and airbursts have resulted in misinterpretations of evidence at Tall el-Hammam', Scientific Reports 15:13869 (22 Apr 2025), Matters Arising.
Retraction Note, Scientific Reports (2025), doi 10.1038/s41598-025-99265-5: the editors 'no longer have confidence that the conclusions presented are reliable.'

LeCompte et al., 'A Tunguska Sized Airburst Destroyed Tall el-Hammam ... (Expanded)', Airbursts and Cratering Impacts (ScienceOpen, 2025), doi 10.14293/ACI.2025.0003. Whether this journal is editorially independent of the authors' group was not verified.
Editor's note (2023): Scientific Reports told readers it was looking into concerns about the paper, two years before the retraction (reported by Retraction Watch, 23 April 2025).
published_press: Sci.News report (29 Sep 2021) quoting James Kennett that there is 'no scientific proof that this destroyed city is indeed the Sodom of the Old Testament.'
Religion News Service (20 Apr 2022) on the debate, quoting Collins that the findings are 'sure evidence'.
claims.for: The 2021 paper reported a city-wide, roughly 1.5 m carbon-and-ash-rich destruction layer containing shocked quartz (about 5-10 GPa), melted pottery and mudbrick, diamond-like carbon, soot, iron- and silicon-rich spherules, carbonate spherules from melted plaster, and melted platinum, iridium, nickel, gold, silver, zircon, chromite and quartz; heating experiments implied temperatures above 2000 C. It argued the blast levelled more than 12 m of a multi-storey palace and a 4 m mudbrick rampart, fragmented human skeletons, and dumped about 4 wt% salt that caused a 300-600 year abandonment of about 120 settlements. The 2025 expanded version adds EBSD and TEM evidence it says shows planar deformation features and high-pressure phases diagnostic of shock, plus a directional debris pattern. Eleven of the authors (including LeCompte, Kennett, West and Silvia) formally disagree with the retraction.
claims.against: Jaret and Harris (American Museum of Natural History; Fernbank Science Center) argue the paper did not follow established criteria for shocked minerals and that its melt and high-temperature evidence means little in archaeological debris from a people with ceramic and smelting technology; much of the 'melt glass' is remelted pottery. Boslough (University of New Mexico) and Bruno (Indiana University) show the Tunguska comparisons rest on misquoted and exaggerated sources (for example the '>80 million trees' figure) and that a Tunguska-sized airburst cannot produce the claimed ground temperatures or winds at the distances required. The image manipulation correction (2022) and the Tunguska correction (2023) preceded the 2025 retraction, which cites Jaret and Harris and Boslough and Bruno. Critics also noted that eight of the 21 authors founded the Comet Research Group (Science Integrity Digest, as reported by RNS). Christian critics who reject the Tall el-Hammam identification on chronological grounds (Wood, Merrill, Turpin) reject the airburst as an explanation of Sodom for the same reason: wrong date.

claims.name: Bab edh-Dhra
claims.coord_source: OpenStreetMap node 3637064328, tagged historic=archaeological_site, name:en 'Bab edh-Dhra'.
claims.claim: The Early Bronze Age walled town of Bab edh-Dhra, on the Lisan peninsula southeast of the Dead Sea, is Sodom, destroyed by fire at the end of Early Bronze III.
claims.text: The five cities are Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar), allied in 'the valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea)' (Genesis 14:2-3). Lot fled to Zoar (Genesis 19). Fire and brimstone fell from heaven and the smoke rose 'like the smoke of a furnace' (Genesis 19:24-28).
claims.who: Excavated by Walter Rast and Thomas Schaub (Expedition to the Dead Sea Plain, founded 1973); cemetery excavated earlier by Paul Lapp (1965-1967). The identification with Sodom is argued by Bryant G. Wood (Associates for Biblical Research), Bible and Spade 1999 and 2007. Rast and Schaub themselves suggested, per the BAR sidebar, that the visible ruins may have inspired the story; Rast's 1987 chapter 'Bab edh-Dhra and the Origin of the Sodom Saga' (in Archaeology and Biblical Interpretation, ed. Perdue, Toombs and Johnson) was not opened.
claims.digging: Surveyed 1973; town site and region excavated in a series of seasons 1975-1990 (ASOR tribute). Publications: Bab edh-Dhra: Excavations in the Cemetery Directed by Paul Lapp (1989) and Bab edh-Dhra: Excavations at the Town Site 1975-1981 (2003, reissued 2021). The EDSP, now co-directed by Meredith S. Chesson and Morag M. Kersel, reported publication work for 2022-2023 (Archaeology in Jordan 4, 2024). No new fieldwork in 2025-2026 was verified; current work found is publication of old excavations.
published_peer: Rast and Schaub (and team), Bab edh-Dhra: Excavations at the Town Site (1975-1981), Eisenbrauns 2003; reissued Penn State University Press 2021 (excavation report, cited via ASOR).
Chesson, Kersel et al., 'Expedition to the Dead Sea Plain (EDSP): Publication Efforts of EDSP Excavations at Bab adh-Dhra and Numayra', Archaeology in Jordan 4: 2022-2023 (ACOR, 2024), 116-118.
published_press: Bryant G. Wood, 'The Discovery of the Sin Cities of Sodom and Gomorrah', Bible and Spade 12:3 (Summer 1999); ABR ministry magazine.
Bryant G. Wood, 'Locating Sodom: A Critique of the Northern Proposal', Bible and Spade 20:3 (Summer 2007).
claims.for: Wood argues: Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira were the only inhabited towns in the region from about 3300 to 900 BC; Bab edh-Dhra's charnel houses were burned at the end of the town's life, and in charnel house A22 the fire started in the roof and burned inward, which he reads as fire falling from above (Genesis 19:24); Numeira was buried in ash up to 0.40 m deep with burned roofs and skeletons; both sit on the eastern fault line, so an earthquake could have forced bitumen and petroleum to the surface and ignited it; seeds point to a late spring or early summer destruction; the southern location fits Genesis 10:19, the Valley of Siddim, Ezekiel 16:46 and the ancient placement of Zoar. On date, he notes the excavators put the end of EB III at about 2350 BC (Rast) or 2300 BC (Schaub), against his biblical date of about 2070 BC, and argues EB III has no firm Egyptian synchronisms so the gap may close.
claims.against: The excavators' own dates leave a gap of roughly 230-280 years from Wood's biblical date (Wood concedes this; BiblePlaces says more than 200 years). Later work separates the two destructions: one summary puts Numeira about 2600 BC and Bab edh-Dhra about 2350 BC (as reported in secondary sources; not verified in the primary report). James Hoffmeier says Rast and Schaub's association of these sites with Sodom and Gomorrah was 'evaluated by the discipline and rejected.' Collins argues the sites are too small (about 12 acres), that nothing in the text points south, and that their destruction is far too early. Answers in Genesis and Wood both reject Tall el-Hammam, but that does not make the southern case: Kris Udd's dissertation and Nate Wilson's critique (linked by BiblePlaces) question whether the sites can be identified as Sodom at all. Wood's own survey found that Safi, Feifa and Khanazir, the other proposed 'cities', turned out to be a cemetery, an Iron Age fort and EB IV tombs, so only two of five cities have candidates.

A church summary reports lab results showing an evaporite (gypsum-type) deposit, not burned buildings, but names no lab. Critics on all sides, including creationist organisations who share his belief in a literal Sodom, reject the claim.

topics.name: Joshua's altar on Mount Ebal
topics.intro: Moses tells Israel to set up plastered stones and an altar on Mount Ebal once they have crossed the Jordan, and to read the blessings and the curses from Gerizim and Ebal (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27). Joshua does it (Joshua 8:30-35). In the 1980s Adam Zertal dug a stone structure on the mountain that he read as that altar, and in 2022 a small folded lead tablet sifted from his spoil heaps was announced as a curse text. Both readings are argued over.

claims.name: Mount Ebal structure (el-Burnat)
claims.coord_source: OpenStreetMap node 4974025556, tagged historic=archaeological_site, name 'mizbeah Har Eival' (Mount Ebal altar), on the northeast side of Mount Ebal above Nablus. Not checked against Zertal's published grid reference.
claims.claim: The Iron Age I stone structure that Adam Zertal excavated on the northeast slope of Mount Ebal is the altar Joshua built there (Joshua 8:30-31), or at least an early Israelite altar.
claims.text: Moses commands: 'you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal' (Deuteronomy 11:29); 'you shall set up on Mount Ebal, these stones ... and coat them with lime. Moreover, you shall build there an altar to Yahweh your God, an altar of stones; you shall not wield an iron tool on them' (Deuteronomy 27:4-5), with burnt offerings and peace offerings and the law written on the stones (27:6-8). 'Then Joshua built an altar to Yahweh, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal ... an altar of uncut stones' and wrote a copy of the law on the stones, then read 'the blessing and the curse' with half the people in front of Gerizim and half in front of Ebal (Joshua 8:30-35).
claims.who: Adam Zertal (University of Haifa) found the site in 1980 during the Manasseh Hill Country Survey and excavated it 1982-1989 (dates per Stripling et al. 2023 and Hawkins 2007). Supporters of a cultic reading include Michael Coogan (BAR) and Ralph K. Hawkins (dissertation, Andrews University 2007; book, Eisenbrauns 2012). The leading early opponent was Aharon Kempinski. Scott Stripling (ABR) argues that a smaller, earlier round installation beneath the rectangular structure is a Late Bronze Age altar.
claims.digging: Zertal excavated 1982-1989. No new stratigraphic excavation since. In December 2019 an ABR team led by Stripling wet-sifted Zertal's dump piles. In June 2023, per Emek Shaveh, about 80 cubic metres of soil were removed from the site under army escort and taken to Shavei Shomron for sifting, a project Emek Shaveh says was approved by the Civil Administration's Staff Officer for Archaeology but not licensed by the Palestinian Department of Antiquities, which it says holds licensing authority in Area B. No 2025-2026 fieldwork was verified.

claims.for: The main structure is a nearly square stone construction of about 24.5 by 29.5 feet, with unhewn fieldstone walls about 5 feet thick and 9 feet high laid on bedrock, with no floor and no entrance, deliberately filled with stones, earth and ash; animal bones in the fill matched, in Zertal's view, the sacrifices of Leviticus 1; a 23-foot inclined 'ramp' fits Exodus 20:26 (no steps to the altar); two corners align north-south within less than one degree; there is little domestic pottery. Two Egyptian scarabs of Ramesses II help date the founding, and Iron Age I pottery (about 1200-1000 BC) the use. The site is on Ebal, the mountain the text names, and Hawkins concluded it 'appears to fit the criteria for a cultic site.'
claims.against: Aharon Kempinski read three Iron Age I phases: pits and silos, then a farmhouse, then the house filled in as the base of a watchtower; the 'ramp' is a collapsed wall and the nearby walls are house walls. Emek Shaveh (2021) states Zertal's theory was rejected by most archaeologists, and that other views see a lookout tower or an altar that is not Joshua's; it names no scholars. Even scholars who accept a cultic site do not thereby accept 'Joshua's altar': Joshua 8:31-32 describes an altar of uncut stones with the law written on plastered stones, and no inscription was found in situ. The Iron Age I date is also later than the early-date (15th century BC) conquest that many conservative critics hold, which is why Stripling now points to the earlier round installation instead.

claims.name: Mount Ebal lead 'curse tablet'
claims.coord_source: Findspot is the east dump pile beside Zertal's excavation at el-Burnat; coordinate is the site point, OpenStreetMap node 4974025556. The object was found in sifted dump, not in situ.
claims.claim: A tiny folded lead tablet sifted from Zertal's Mount Ebal dump carries a Late Bronze Age proto-alphabetic curse naming the God YHW, the earliest Hebrew inscription, tying the site to the curses of Deuteronomy 27 and Joshua 8.
claims.text: 'the curse on Mount Ebal' (Deuteronomy 11:29); Joshua 'read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse' (Joshua 8:34); writing on stones at Ebal (Deuteronomy 27:8; Joshua 8:32). Scripture mentions writing on stones, not on lead.
claims.who: Found December 2019 by wet-sifting specialist Frankie Snyder in an Associates for Biblical Research team led by Scott Stripling. Announced at a press release datelined Houston, 24 March 2022. Peer-reviewed paper: Stripling (The Bible Seminary, Katy), Gershon Galil (University of Haifa), Ivana Kumpova, Jaroslav Valach, Daniel Vavrik (Institute of Theoretical and Applied Mechanics, Czech Academy of Sciences), Pieter Gert van der Veen (Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz), Heritage Science, online 12 May 2023.
claims.digging: No excavation; the object came from sifting Zertal's 1980s dump (December 2019). A further sifting operation took place in June 2023 (see ebal-zertal-altar). The authors said a later article would publish the exterior text; no such peer-reviewed article was found. No 2025-2026 work verified.

published_press: ABR press release via RNS distribution, 24 March 2022: claimed 40 letters, a curse invoking YHW, peer-reviewed article 'in process'.

Gershon Galil, The Mount Ebal Inscription (Megillat Sefer Press, 2024), reported to present the exterior 'Outer A' text as 46 letters in 13 words; the book page could not be opened (HTTP 500), so this is unverified.

claims.for: X-ray tomography at Telc (Czech Academy of Sciences) showed, according to the authors, writing on both exterior and interior. Galil read the interior ('Inner B') as 48 letters in 14 word sets: 'You are cursed by the god YHW, cursed. You will die, cursed ... Cursed you are by YHW', with 'arur ('cursed') six times, in a chiastic pattern, dated to Late Bronze II (about 1400-1200 BC, no later than about 1250 BC). The lead came from Lavrion in Greece, a mine in use in the Late Bronze Age (analysis by Naama Yahalom-Mack). The dump came from structures Zertal dated to LB II and Iron I. Stripling says he is 'confident that there is writing on the tablet', that known net sinkers have rope grooves this object lacks, and that the rarity of such finds reflects how rarely dumps are wet-sifted; ABR (Bryan Windle) notes Mazar does not explain how a net sinker reached a mountain far from water in a cultic context.
claims.against: Maeir and Rollston: the published images 'fail to demonstrate any discernible letters', photos and drawings do not match, and the marks are 'random scratches, striations, pitting and indentations'; most conclusions lack an empirical basis. Amihai Mazar sees no clear letters and identifies a lead fishing-net sinker. Yahalom-Mack (who did the lead analysis) says Lavrion was worked from the fourth millennium BC to the Roman period, so the lead source cannot securely date the object. Haughwout (a Bible college scholar, i.e. a critic sharing the authors' starting beliefs) concludes there is insufficient epigraphic evidence that writing exists at all; if four letters exist they might read 'depths'; it could be a clasp, a weight or a Roman lead tessera; a dump-pile find cannot be dated by context. Kletter argues Galil 'did not restore an ancient inscription, but created a new' one, picking marks that fit and dropping those that do not; the 'letters' vary hugely in size and face every direction. Even within the team, van der Veen published more conservative drawings than Galil and reportedly called Galil's reading a 'fantasy reading'; the paper itself notes that Galil alone holds all 48 letters to be clear. The letter count moved from 40 (2022 press release) to 48 (2023 paper). Political context affecting access: the site is in Area B; Maeir told ToI there is 'political background noise' around the claim; Emek Shaveh says the 2019 and 2023 soil removals were unlicensed by the Palestinian antiquities authority.

topics.name: Bethsaida
topics.intro: Bethsaida was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44), near where Jesus fed the five thousand (Luke 9:10) and healed a blind man (Mark 8:22). Josephus says Philip the tetrarch rebuilt it as a city and named it Julias. Two sites near the north shore of the Sea of Galilee are dug as Bethsaida by rival teams, and much of the argument turns on where the shoreline was in the first century.

claims.name: et-Tell
claims.coord_source: OpenStreetMap way 734139729, tagged historic=archaeological_site, archaeological_site=city, name:en 'Bethsaida', name:he 'Tel Beit Tsaida' (centroid as returned by Nominatim).
claims.claim: The 20-acre mound of et-Tell, about 1.5 km north of the Sea of Galilee near the Jordan inflow, is New Testament Bethsaida, renamed Julias by Herod Philip, and earlier was the Iron Age capital of Geshur.
claims.text: Jesus sent the disciples by boat 'to the other side to Bethsaida' (Mark 6:45); 'they came to Bethsaida' and a blind man was brought (Mark 8:22); 'He slipped away by Himself to a city called Bethsaida' (Luke 9:10); 'Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter' (John 1:44); 'Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee' (John 12:21). Mark arrives by boat; Luke calls it a city; John places it 'of Galilee'. None gives a precise location.
claims.who: Rami Arav, director of the Bethsaida Excavations Project since 1987; the consortium was housed at the University of Nebraska Omaha (founded 1990, publishing since 1991). The Nelson Glueck School of Biblical Archaeology (HUC-JIR, Jerusalem) now describes the consortium as 'formerly associated with the University of Nebraska and now under the auspices of the NGSBA'.
claims.digging: Arav began work in 1987 (BAS; ToI 2017); seasonal excavation through the following decades (Arav in 2017: 'under seasonal archaeological excavations for the past 30 years'). The NGSBA page says 'Excavations at the site are still underway', but it is undated. No 2025 or 2026 et-Tell season report could be found or verified.
published_peer: R. Steven Notley, 'Et-Tell Is Not Bethsaida', Near Eastern Archaeology 70.4 (2007), 220-230 (cited; not opened).
Rami Arav, 'Bethsaida: A Response to Steven Notley', Near Eastern Archaeology 74 (2011), 92-100, with Notley's reply and Arav's rejoinder, 74:2 (2011), 103-104 (cited; not opened).
published_press: Rami Arav, 'Bethsaida Controversy', The Bible and Interpretation, August 2017 (online essay).
Arav, 'Searching for Bethsaida: The Case for Et-Tell', BAR 46:2 (2020) (cited in the companion el-Araj article; not opened).
NGSBA project page (site summary by the excavation's institutional home).
claims.for: Arav and the NGSBA summary: the tel was founded in the Early Bronze Age, with major Iron Age fortifications; in the 9th century BC a 6 m wall and the largest Iron Age city gate excavated in Israel (inner gatehouse 35 by 17.5 m) with a basalt gate altar and a stele of a horned bull, and a palace; this is taken as the capital of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3; 14:32), destroyed by Tiglath-pileser III in 734 BC. Geomorphology shows the plain below was once part of the lake and silted up, so the town, originally on the shore, ended up about 1.5 km inland, a process the NGSBA page says continued until the Hellenistic period, while Arav in 2017 places the shoreline's withdrawal in a 4th century AD geological event. Hellenistic and Roman courtyard houses yielded net weights, iron anchors, needles and fishhooks (a fishing economy), a cellar with wine amphorae, limestone vessels typical of Jewish settlement, and early 1st century AD a 20 by 6 m building with limestone ashlars and two bronze incense shovels, which Arav identifies as the temple Philip built for Julia Livia when he refounded the town as Julias about AD 30 (Josephus, Antiquities 18). Arav says the place-name committee of Israel's Prime Minister's office confirmed et-Tell as Bethsaida.
claims.against: Notley argues et-Tell is too far from the lake (about 1.5 miles) and too high to be the fishing village from which Peter, Andrew and Philip came and to which boats sailed (Mark 6:45). The el-Araj team points to an unexplained drop in material culture at et-Tell at the start of the early Roman period and says twenty years of work there are 'far from conclusive' for first century Bethsaida. Jodi Magness, an archaeologist and National Geographic grantee, told National Geographic that 'the Roman period remains are very poor, and therefore the site does not look like an urban center.' The NGSBA summary itself says only 'very fragmentary remains of the foundations' survive of the proposed temple and offers it as 'Perhaps' Philip's temple.

claims.claim: The lakeshore site of el-Araj, about 2 km from et-Tell, is first century Bethsaida (Julias), and its Byzantine basilica is the Church of the Apostles built over the house of Peter and Andrew.
claims.text: Bethsaida is reached by boat (Mark 6:45), is 'the city of Andrew and Peter' and Philip's home (John 1:44), and is 'of Galilee' (John 12:21). Scripture says nothing about a church; that tradition is later (Willibald, 8th century).

Steven Notley (then Nyack College; now Pillar College, New Jersey), academic director, with Dina Shalem; the El Araj Excavation Project, now presented as 'Bethsaida-Julias' under the Center for the Study of Ancient Judaism and Christian Origins (CSAJCO). Supporters named in the 2022 press release include Museum of the Bible and the Lanier Theological Library Foundation.
claims.digging: Survey from 2014 and excavation since 2016. Roman bathhouse found in early seasons (BAS says 2016 work; Notley and Aviam date it to 2017); monastery and basilica announced July 2019; donor inscription (Inscription 3) announced August 2022. A July 2025 wildfire exposed Roman structures; a second 2025 session was planned for October. 2026 is the tenth season: summer sessions in July 2026 (Lanier Center reports, posted September 2026, describing Herodian lamps, chalk vessels, a Roman domestic tabun, fresco fragments and a Doric capital fragment) and a fall session scheduled 9-23 October 2026 (results not yet verified). Active now.

claims.for: The site sits on the lakeshore near the Jordan estuary, where Josephus puts Julias, which suits a fishing village reached by boat; the excavators say their finds show the first century lake was lower than once thought, close to its modern level, so el-Araj was on the shore. Finds: a Jewish fishing village of the 1st century BC to 1st century AD with net weights; a Roman bathhouse with mosaic fragments and a silver Nero coin of AD 65-66, which they read as Philip's upgrade of the village to a polis; a Roman residence and coins; in 2026 Herodian lamps and chalk vessels, indicators of a Second Temple Jewish population. In 2019 a monastery and a basilica (about 88 by 52 feet) with ornate mosaics were found, matching the pilgrim Willibald's 725 report of a church over Peter's house at Bethsaida. Inscription 3 in the diaconicon asks Peter, 'chief of the apostles and holder of the heavenly keys', to intercede for the donor Constantine and his children George and Theophano; Notley called this 'our strongest indicator that Peter had a special association with the basilica.' Earlier, Mendel Nun and Bargil Pixner favoured el-Araj (Pixner as the fishing quarter of a two-part Bethsaida).
claims.against: Arav (2017) says he dug el-Araj in 1987 and found, under the Byzantine layer, only beach deposits barren of pottery, and that ground-penetrating radar along the shore showed no habitation layer, so the Roman remains are small; he proposes the bathhouse belonged to a camp of Agrippa II's mercenaries, notes that Roman bathhouses do not appear in Jewish towns of the region before the late Roman period, calls the conclusions 'extremely premature', and argues el-Araj was a Byzantine-period Bethsaida (perhaps 'New Bethsaida') after the shore moved south. He adds that Capernaum's excavators Corbo and Loffreda thought Willibald's church description fits Capernaum, and that Byzantine pilgrims 'cared very little about authenticities'. Arav also told ToI the Roman layer 'is not enough to identify a place with Bethsaida.' Lake level is disputed: BAS (2023) reports groundwater flooding the lowest levels; Franz reports Mendel Nun's view that ancient lake levels were lower, so more of the site was dry land than once assumed, while Arav's 1987 square found only beach deposits under the Byzantine level. Where the 1st century shoreline lay is the crux, and no peer-reviewed lake-level study was verified here. Even the sympathetic BAS writer (2019) called the Church of the Apostles reasoning close to tautological, since it assumes el-Araj is Bethsaida; the Peter inscription is dated by letter forms to the second half of the 6th century or later, so it shows Byzantine belief, not 1st century identity.

topics.name: The crowd at Pentecost
topics.intro: Pentecost was the Feast of Weeks, one of the three feasts when Jewish men went up to Jerusalem, and Luke says the city was full of devout Jews "from every nation under heaven" (Acts 2:5). Then the crowd lists itself: fifteen peoples and lands, running roughly east to west from Parthia to Rome, with Cretans and Arabs added at the end. Most were Jews whose families had lived abroad since the exile, and Luke adds proselytes, Gentiles who had become Jews. Each line runs from the homeland to Jerusalem to show where the crowd came from; it isn't the road anyone took. Some of them went home with the message, and Peter's first letter is written to believers in Pontus, Cappadocia and Asia (1 Peter 1:1).

nations.then: The Parthian Empire, Rome's rival in the east. The pin is its capital, Ctesiphon on the Tigris (Pleiades 893976).
Media, the highlands around Ecbatana, by then a province of Parthia.
Elam, the old kingdom around Susa at the head of the Persian Gulf.
The land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, home of the Babylonian Jews since the exile.
